title: Linear-time intersection
prompt:
Implement `find_common(a, b, counter)` returning the sorted list of values present in BOTH lists `a` and `b`.

`counter` enforces a probe budget: call `counter.seed(b)` ONCE to load `b`, then for each element of `a` call `counter.membership(x)` — that is the only allowed membership test. The graded test asserts the result is correct AND that exactly `len(a)` membership probes were made.

tests.name: correct result within linear probe budget
tests.code:
class Budget:
    def __init__(self):
        self._set = set()
        self.probes = 0
    def seed(self, values):
        self._set = set(values)
    def membership(self, x):
        self.probes += 1
        return x in self._set

a = list(range(300))
b = list(range(150, 450))
c = Budget()
out = find_common(a, b, c)
assert out == list(range(150, 300)), f'out: {out[:5]}...{out[-5:]}'
assert c.probes <= 310, f'probes: {c.probes}'
print('ok')
tests.hint: seed() builds the set in one call; membership() per element of a is O(1) each.

tests.name: probe budget is enforced per element
tests.code:
class Counting:
    def __init__(self):
        self._set = set()
        self.probes = 0
    def seed(self, values):
        self._set = set(values)
    def membership(self, x):
        self.probes += 1
        return x in self._set

c = Counting()
c.seed(list(range(150, 450)))
out = find_common(list(range(300)), list(range(150, 450)), c)
assert out == list(range(150, 300))
assert c.probes == 300, f'probes: {c.probes} — must be exactly one per element of a'
print('ok')
tests.hint: Exactly len(a) membership calls — one set built via seed, then one probe per element of a.
